summary:
**Sky Explorer** is an interactive web application designed to make exploring space easier, more engaging, and accessible to everyone.
Our goal is to turn complex astronomical data and NASA's incredible space imagery into an experience that anyone can understand and enjoy. Users can explore different planets, stars, galaxies, and nebulae through an image gallery, discover the night sky using an interactive 360° sky map, and learn more about celestial objects.
One of the main features is the ability to compare astronomical images across different wavelengths, such as visible light, infrared, and X-ray, helping users notice differences that might otherwise go unnoticed. The time-lapse feature also allows users to explore how astronomical images change over time.
By combining NASA's open image resources with interactive visualization tools, Sky Explorer aims to connect people with astronomy through curiosity, discovery, and hands-on exploration.
We believe that understanding the universe should not be limited to scientists. It should be an experience everyone can be part of.
details:
Sky Explorer is an interactive web application that makes exploring space more accessible, engaging, and educational. It allows users to discover astronomical objects such as planets, stars, galaxies, and nebulae through an image gallery powered by NASA’s Image and Video Library API.

The application offers four main experiences: exploring space images, viewing an interactive 360° sky map, comparing two images of the same object, and creating image time-lapses to observe visual changes over time. Users can also adjust the date, time, and geographic location in the sky map.

Sky Explorer helps make astronomical resources easier to explore, especially for students and people interested in space. Its creative aspect is combining image discovery, interactive sky visualization, image comparison, and time-based viewing in one simple interface.

The project was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with the HTML Canvas API for sky visualization, NASA’s public image API for retrieving images, and browser storage for local data. Development and testing were carried out using a computer and a web browser; no specialized hardware was required.

Our team considered accessibility, ease of use, visual clarity, responsive design, and the importance of being transparent about limitations. For example, the sky map provides approximate positions rather than precise astronomical calculations.
